title: Bruce Flatt: Strength to Act When Others Cannot

reader_summary.source_label: From the episode notes — transcript not yet available
reader_summary.headline: Bruce Flatt explains how to buy assets when others cannot due to a shortage of capital.
reader_summary.overview: This episode profiles Bruce Flatt, who led Brookfield Corporation from 2002. He argues that the best time to invest is when capital is scarce and others are fearful. Flatt uses long-term debt and buys assets below their replacement cost to protect his company.

key_points.text: Flatt states that the clearest signal to buy is a shortage of capital when few others can bid.
key_points.evidence_quote: the clearest signal to buy is a shortage of capital

key_points.text: Brookfield finances each asset with long-term non-recourse debt so one loan failure does not force a sale elsewhere.
key_points.evidence_quote: Brookfield finances each asset on its own, with long-term non-recourse debt, so no single loan can force a sale elsewhere in the company.

key_points.text: Flatt advises never to get into a situation where you lack capital when things are going down.
key_points.evidence_quote: never, ever, ever get yourself in a situation where you don't have capital when things are going down.

notes: We are delighted to share with you our audio program on Bruce Flatt, chief executive of Brookfield Corporation, part of the Great Investors podcast by Latticework. Each program in the series is an hour-long narrated profile of one investor, researched by the MOI Global team from the investor’s own letters, talks and interviews. We make these programs so that members can learn how a great investor thinks and works, through the decisions he made and what he said about them at the time. Your feedback on what was useful, and on which investors to cover next, shapes what we produce. We start with who he is: Bruce Flatt joined Brookfield in 1990 and succeeded Jack Cockwell as its chief executive in 2002, when the company’s name was Brascan. By his own account he was a value investor at heart from the start. Brascan became Brookfield Asset Management, his letter for 2005 reported. In December 2022 the parent became Brookfield Corporation and handed shares of its asset manager, which kept the old name, to its shareholders. In February 2026 Connor Teskey became chief executive of Brookfield Asset Management, and Flatt stayed on as chair of its board. He argues that the clearest signal to buy is a shortage of capital. In a distressed period, he wrote in his letter for 2009, the owner has too much debt, cash flow has shrunk, the mood is gloomy and financing is scarce, so few can bid. Brookfield finances each asset on its own, with long-term non-recourse debt, so no single loan can force a sale elsewhere in the company. The third of three principles he credits to Jack Cockwell’s generation is to have more capital than anybody else. On September 10, 2025, at Brookfield Asset Management’s investor day, he went on: “never, ever, ever get yourself in a situation where you don’t have capital when things are going down.” Real assets, he wrote on November 5, 2010, behave like bonds, with cash flows far into the future, and like equities, because those cash flows grow. Brookfield buys them below replacement cost: a coal terminal in Australia cost three quarters of that in 2009, two years after its previous owner had paid one and a half times. Downside protection of the capital employed is in a sentence near the end of nearly every annual letter since 2005; in 2025 he said Brookfield’s investment committees spend virtually all their time on it. The miracle of compounding, he said in August 2018, comes down to sticking with it. His letter of February 12, 2026, set down the record: $1 million invested in Brookfield Corporation more than thirty years earlier was worth $285 million, 19 percent a year. The program opens with his letter of November 7, 2008, and the 7.5 million shares Brookfield bought back at an average of US$20. It goes back to the first funds, which nobody would take, and the move out of mining. It tells 2009 through General Growth Properties, whose defaulted bank debt Brookfield bought that year: $2.3 billion invested, $6.0 billion of value by his November 2013 count. It has TerraForm, Westinghouse and a tower on Park Avenue. It has the letter of March 23, 2020, the split of 2022 and the partnership that promotes from within. It ends with the trees Brookfield let grow on the stump and his advice to a young person starting out. The program quotes him from his letters to shareholders first. They run from his first as chief executive in 2002 to his letter of May 14, 2026. Brookfield’s own recordings cover its investor days of 2022 and 2025 and its podcast of October 2024. Beside them are a talk to Google employees in August 2018, a Bloomberg interview in March 2022, Norges Bank Investment Management’s podcast late in 2023 and The Knowledge Project in April 2025. The complete program runs sixty-six minutes. Get the next program the day it comes out. Great Investors is on Apple, Spotify, and YouTube (or add the podcast feed to any app). The transcript is available for download to members only. Narrated by an AI voice. This is a public episode.
